{{Short description|1957 mathematics paper by Alexander Grothendieck}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Grothendieck's ''Tôhoku'' paper}}
The article "'''Sur quelques points d'algèbre homologique'''" by [[Alexander Grothendieck]],{{sfnp|Grothendieck|1957}} now often referred to as the '''Tôhoku paper''',{{sfnp|Schlager|Lauer|2000|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=rB7BjYsD2j4C&pg=PA715 251]|loc="commonly referred to as the Tohoku Paper"}} was published in 1957 in the ''[[Tôhoku Mathematical Journal]]''. It revolutionized the subject of [[homological algebra]], a purely algebraic aspect of [[algebraic topology]].{{sfnp|Chang|2011|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=4siw31DPONUC&pg=PA115 115]|loc="He [...] revolutionized homological algebra in his "Tohoku paper""}} It removed the need to distinguish the cases of [[module (mathematics)|module]]s over a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] and [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaves]] of [[abelian group]]s over a [[topological space]].{{sfnp|Lawvere|2000|p=715|loc="Grothendieck's Tohoku paper [...] showed that this conceptual basis for homological algebra over a ring also applies to linear objects varying as sheaves over a space"}}

==Background==
Material in the paper dates from Grothendieck's year at the [[University of Kansas]] in 1955–56.{{sfnp|Cartier|Illusie|Katz|Laumon|2006|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=_BnSoQSKnNUC&pg=PR7 vii]|loc="his Tôhoku article dates from his visit to Kansas"}} Research there allowed him to put homological algebra on an axiomatic basis, by introducing the [[abelian category]] concept.{{sfnp|Pragacz|2005|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=AqCXg0WtnrEC&pg=PR14 xiv–xv]|loc="Grothendieck constructs his axiomatic theory of ''Abelian categories''. His main result asserts that the sheaves of modules form an Abelian category"}}

That same year, a textbook treatment of homological algebra, ''Homological Algebra'' by [[Henri Cartan]] and [[Samuel Eilenberg]], appeared. Grothendieck's work was largely independent of it; however, his abelian category concept had at least partially been anticipated by others.{{sfnp|nLab|loc="Essentially, they were defined in an earlier paper by Buchsbaum as 'exact categories', with different motivation [...] Saunders MacLane had rudiments of the definition of abelian category, around 1950, but it was a bit different and less invariant notion (and under a different name 'bicategory')"}} [[David Buchsbaum]] in his doctoral thesis written under Eilenberg had introduced a notion of "[[Abelian category#History|exact category]]" close to the abelian category concept (needing only [[direct sum]]s to be identical); and had formulated the idea of "[[enough injectives]]".{{sfnp|Weibel|1999|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=7iRijkz0rrUC&pg=PA815 815]}} The Tôhoku paper contains an argument to prove that a [[Grothendieck category]] (a particular type of abelian category, the name coming later) has enough injectives; the author indicated that the proof was of a standard type.{{sfnp|Neeman|2001|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=WptvM91FrbQC&pg=PA19 19]|loc="Grothendieck said that it had been well-known, and he was merely sketching it"}} In showing by this means that categories of sheaves of abelian groups admitted [[injective resolution]]s, Grothendieck went beyond the theory available in Cartan and Eilenberg's book to prove the existence of a [[cohomology theory]] in generality.{{sfnp|Marquis|2006|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=tVOuvxqhBxwC&pg=PA236 236–7]|loc="Grothendieck solved the problem not by giving an explicit construction, but rather by finding the appropriate categorical framework for homological algebra in general and providing a categorical property from which the construction required could be performed. Grothendieck's work was therefore astonishing not only because it showed how to subsume the cohomological theory of sheaves within homological algebra [...] but also in the way he used categories to obtain this result"}}

==Later developments==
After the [[Gabriel–Popescu theorem]] of 1964, it was known that every Grothendieck category is a [[Quotient of an abelian category|quotient category]] of a [[module category]].{{sfnp|Encyclopedia of Mathematics|loc="A full subcategory 𝔖 of the category <sub>{{math|''R''}}</sub>𝔐 of left {{math|''R''}}-modules [...] An Abelian category is a Grothendieck category if and only if it is equivalent to some quotient category <sub>{{math|''R''}}</sub>𝔐/𝔖"}}

The Tôhoku paper also introduced the [[Grothendieck spectral sequence]] associated to the composition of [[derived functor]]s.{{sfnp|Weibel|1994|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=flm-dBXfZ_gC&pg=PA150 150]|loc="In his classic paper [Tohoku], Grothendieck introduced a spectral sequence associated to the composition of two functors. Today it is one of the organizational principles of Homological Algebra"}} In further reconsideration of the foundations of homological algebra, Grothendieck introduced and developed with [[Jean-Louis Verdier]] the [[derived category]] concept.{{sfnp|Căldăraru|2005|p=[https://books.google.com.ec/books?id=t5wbCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA43&source=gbs_toc_r&cad=2#v=onepage&q&f=false 43]|loc="The derived category is a rather complicated object, having its roots in efforts by Grothendieck and Verdier to put firmer foundations on homological algebra than those originally laid out by Grothendieck in his Tôhoku paper"}} The initial motivation, as announced by Grothendieck at the 1958 [[International Congress of Mathematicians]], was to formulate results on [[coherent duality]], now going under the name "Grothendieck duality".{{sfnp|Neeman|2010|p=[http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download;jsessionid=BB646E964DD6ADFC6527D0110FB4D95C?doi=10.1.1.611.7150&rep=rep1&type=pdf 297]|loc="In his 1958 talk at the Edinburgh ICM Grothendieck announced that he had a solution, but also that the homological algebra language necessary to state it did not yet exist. Verdier’s thesis project was to develop the framework. Derived categories were born in that thesis"}}
